# Page 3^page=3
Today: Chapter 7Tensor Fields 1. Preliminary, 2. Covariant di˙erentiation, 3. Christo˙el symbols, 4. Covariant di˙erentiation of tensors, 5. Ricci's theorem, 6. Rie mann - Christof fel ten sor, 7. Ricci tensor. 1 36

# Page 4^page=4
Reminder

# Page 5^page=5
Generalised Coordinates with local basis Generalised Coordinates with local basis Recall: We are now considering generalised coordinate systems with local bases . A local basis is a basis e1, e2, e3 that varies from point to point: ej = ej(x1, x 2, x 3), e j = e j(x 1, x 2, x 3). 2 36

# Page 6^page=6
Christoffel Symbols and the metric tensor Christo˙el Symbols and the metric tensor Christo˙el symbols of second kind are de˝ned as Γi jk = e i · ∂ej ∂xk . Christo˙el symbols of ˝rst kind are de˝ned as Γijk = ei · ∂ej ∂xk . Christo˙el symbols of the ˝rst and second kind are related via the metric tensor Γijk = giℓΓ ℓ jk, Γ i jk = giℓΓℓkj. 3 36

# Page 7^page=7
Γ i jk as expansion coefficients Christo˙el symbols as expansion coe˚cients Recall that the partial derivatives ∂A ∂xk of any vector A are vectors. Thus, we can expand each ∂A ∂xk with respect to a basis e1, e2, e3, and with respect with its dual e1, e2, e3. It turns out that the Γi jk are the expansion coe˚cients of the vector ∂ej ∂xk with respect to the basis e1, e2, e3: ∂ej ∂xk = Γ 1 jke1 + Γ2 jke2 + Γ3 jke3 = Γ i jkei. 4 36

# Page 8^page=8
Christoffel symbols of first kind Christo˙el symbols of ˝rst kind The same way Γi jk are the expansion coe˚cients of the vector ∂ej ∂xk with respect to the basis e1, e2, e3: ∂ej ∂xk = Γ 1 jke1 + Γ2 jke2 + Γ3 jke3 = Γ i jkei, we can also expand the vector ∂ej ∂xk with respect to the dual basis e1, e2, e3. The new coe˚cients are denoted by Γijk. That is ∂ej ∂xk = Γ1jke 1 + Γ2jke 2 + Γ3jke 3 = Γijke i. These new symbols are called the Christo˙el symbols of the ˝rst kind . 5 36

# Page 9^page=9
Properties of Christoffel symbols Properties of Christo˙el symbols Symmetry in the last two indices: The Christo˙el symbols Γi jk and Γijk are symmetric in the indices j and k. That is Γijk = Γikj, and Γi jk = Γ i kj. They are not tensors ! We have a formulae relating Christo˙el symbols to the metric tensor : Γijk = 1 2 ( ∂gij ∂xk + ∂gik ∂xj − ∂gjk ∂xi ) , Γ i · jk = 1 2 giℓ ( ∂gℓj ∂xk + ∂gℓk ∂xj − ∂gjk ∂xℓ ) . 6 36

# Page 10^page=10
Ricci's Theorem: Ricci's Theorem. The covariant derivative of the metric tensor gik vanishes. Useful formula Ricci's theorem yields the following useful formula ∂gik ∂xℓ = Γikℓ + Γkiℓ. In particular, in orthogonal coordinates Γikℓ + Γkiℓ = 0 =⇒ Γikℓ = −Γkiℓ. 7 36

# Page 11^page=11
Riemann-Christoffel tensor

# Page 12^page=12
Defining spaces De˝ning spaces So far we have only been (mostly) dealing with the usual 1 Euclidean space R3, whether we used Cartesian coordinates or generalised coordinates. However there are other types of spaces. For example: the surface of a sphere is a two-dimensional non-Euclidean space. Question: How can we distinguish between di˙erent spaces? 1 A Euclidean vector space is a ˝nite-dimensional inner product space over the real numbers. 8 36

# Page 13^page=13
Curvature Curvature One way of distinguishing these spaces is to use curvature : Euclidean space has zero curvature, The surface of a sphere has positive curvature, Hyperbolic space has negative curvature. Question: Is there a condition that tells us when a space must be Euclidean? In other words, can we determine whether a space has zero curvature or not? 9 36

# Page 14^page=14
Partial derivatives Partial derivatives Let A be a vector ˝eld with components Ai(x1, x2, x3). The partial derivative of a component is written as ∂Ai ∂xj . Since each component Ai = Ai(x1, x2, x3) is a function, we are simply taking a partial derivatice of a function. For smooth functions, partial derivatives always commute ∂ ∂xk ( ∂Ai ∂xj ) = ∂ ∂xj ( ∂Ai ∂xk ) . 10 36

# Page 15^page=15
Partial derivatives vs tensors A key issue A vector ˝eld is not merely a collection of component functions. It is a geometric object whose components change under a change of coordinates. (I.e. a tensor.) If we compute ∂Ai ∂xj , for each component, the result does not transform as a tensor under general coordinate changes. Therefore, to di˙erentiate vector ˝elds in a way that respects the tensor properties, we need a di˙erent notion of derivative . 11 36

# Page 16^page=16
Covariant derivatives Covariant derivatives To make distinction between both concepts, recall that we denote the covariant derivative of Ai by Ai,j. To stress out this distinction even more, write Ai,j := ∇jAi. We have seen that Ai,j := ∇jAi = ∂Ai ∂xj − Γ k ijAk. (Week 26.2) ▶ The partial derivative di˙erentiates the components. ▶ The Christo˙el symbols correct for the change of basis. ▶ The result transforms as a tensor. 12 36

# Page 17^page=17
The Euclidean special case Euclidean space in Cartesian coordinates In Euclidean space with Cartesian coordinates, ∇jAi = ∂Ai ∂xj . This is because Γ k ij = 0. This is why partial and covariant derivatives appear identical in vector calculus. 13 36

# Page 18^page=18
Second derivatives Second derivatives Second partial derivatives always commute: ∂ ∂xk ( ∂Ai ∂xj ) = ∂ ∂xj ( ∂Ai ∂xk ) . Second covariant derivatives are written as Ai, kj := ∇k∇jAi. There is no reason for these to commute in general. That is ∇k∇jAi ̸= ∇j∇kAi, equivalently Ai, jk ̸= Ai, kj. 14 36

# Page 19^page=19
Curvature Next steps We will show that Ai,jk − Ai,kj is a tensor. This tensor is called Riemann-Christo˙el tensor . To check if we are in Euclidean space , we check if the space has zero curvature. By the above, this amounts to verifying whether the Riemann-Christo˙el tensor is zero. Summary Partial derivatives always commute. Covariant derivatives commute i˙ curvature is zero. Curvature measures the failure of covariant derivatives to commute. 15 36

# Page 20^page=20
RiemannChristoffel tensor RiemannChristo˙el To check whether we are in Euclidean space , we check whether the space has zero curvature. That is, whether covariant derivatives commute: ∇j∇kAi = ∇k∇jAi. We de˝ne the RiemannChristo˙el tensor by Rr ijkAr = ∇j∇kAi − ∇k∇jAi. We now derive a coordinate formula for Rr ijk. 16 36

# Page 21^page=21
Deriving the RiemannChristoffel tensor Deriving the RiemannChristo˙el tensor Recall the general formula for covariant di˙erentiation of a second-rank tensor ∇jTik = ∂Tik ∂xj − Γ p ijTpk − Γ p kjTip. We apply this to Tik = ∇kAi, obtaining ∇j∇kAi = ∂(∇kAi) ∂xj − Γ p ij∇kAp − Γ p kj∇pAi. 17 36

# Page 22^page=22
Deriving the RiemannChristoffel tensor  Part 2 Deriving the RiemannChristo˙el tensor Again ∇j∇kAi = ∂(∇kAi) ∂xj − Γ p ij∇kAp − Γ p kj∇pAi. Recall that ∇kAi = ∂Ai ∂xk − Γ r kiAr. Substituting, ∇j∇kAi = ∂ ∂xj ( ∂Ai ∂xk − Γ r kiAr ) − Γp ij ( ∂Ap ∂xk − Γr kpAr ) − Γp kj ( ∂Ai ∂xp − Γr piAr ) . 18 36

# Page 23^page=23
Deriving the RiemannChristoffel tensor  Part 3 Deriving the RiemannChristo˙el tensor Expanding, ∇j∇kAi = ∂ ∂xj ( ∂Ai ∂xk − Γ r kiAr ) − Γp ij ( ∂Ap ∂xk − Γr kpAr ) − Γp kj ( ∂Ai ∂xp − Γr piAr ) = ∂2Ai ∂xj∂xk − Γ r ki ∂Ar ∂xj − Ar ∂Γr ki ∂xj − Γ p ij ∂Ap ∂xk − Γp kj ∂Ai ∂xp + (Γ p ijΓr kp + Γp kjΓ r pi) Ar. Interchanging j and k gives the formula for ∇k∇jAi. 19 36

# Page 24^page=24
Deriving the RiemannChristoffel tensor  Part 4 Deriving the RiemannChristo˙el tensor Recall that ∇j∇kAi is given by ∂2Ai ∂xj∂xk − Γ r ki ∂Ar ∂xj − Ar ∂Γ r ki ∂xj − Γ p ij ∂Ap ∂xk − Γ p kj ∂Ai ∂xp + Γp ijΓ r pkAr + Γp kjΓ r piAr. We ˝nd a formula for ∇j∇kAi − ∇k∇jAi, by observing each of the following di˙erent types of terms: terms involving second derivatives of A, terms involving ˝rst derivatives of A, terms depending only on the Christo˙el symbols. 20 36

# Page 25^page=25
Deriving the RiemannChristoffel tensor  Part 5 Second derivatives Recall that ∇j∇kAi is given by ∂2Ai ∂xj∂xk − Γ r ki ∂Ar ∂xj − Ar ∂Γ r ki ∂xj − Γ p ij ∂Ap ∂xk − Γ p kj ∂Ai ∂xp + Γ p ijΓ r pkAr + Γ p kjΓ r piAr. Thus, the terms of ∇j∇kAi − ∇k∇jAi involving second derivatives of A are ∂2Ai ∂xj∂xk − ∂2Ai ∂xk∂xj . Since partial derivatives commute, this term vanishes: ∂2Ai ∂xj∂xk − ∂2Ai ∂xk∂xj = 0. 21 36

# Page 26^page=26
Deriving the RiemannChristoffel tensor  Part 6 First derivatives Recall that ∇j∇kAi is given by ∂2Ai ∂xj∂xk −Γ r ki ∂Ar ∂xj − Ar ∂Γ r ki ∂xj −Γ p ij ∂Ap ∂xk − Γ p kj ∂Ai ∂xp + Γp ijΓ r pkAr + Γp kjΓ r piAr. Thus, the terms of ∇j∇kAi − ∇k∇jAi involving ˝rst derivatives of A are ( − Γ r ki ∂Ar ∂xj − Γ p ij ∂Ap ∂xk − Γ p kj ∂Ai ∂xp ) − ( − Γ r ji ∂Ar ∂xk − Γ p ik ∂Ap ∂xj − Γ p jk ∂Ai ∂xp ) . Rearranging, (−Γ r ki ∂Ar ∂xj + Γp ik ∂Ap ∂xj ) ︸ ︷︷ ︸ =0, because Γℓ ik=Γℓ ki + (−Γ p ij ∂Ap ∂xk + Γr ji ∂Ar ∂xk ) ︸ ︷︷ ︸ =0, because Γℓ ij =Γℓ ji + (−Γ p kj ∂Ai ∂xp + Γp jk ∂Ai ∂xp ) ︸ ︷︷ ︸ =0, because Γℓ kj =Γℓ jk . 22 36

# Page 27^page=27
Deriving the RiemannChristoffel tensor  Part 7 Remaining terms Recall that ∇j∇kAi is given by ∂2Ai ∂xj∂xk − Γ r ki ∂Ar ∂xj −Ar ∂Γ r ki ∂xj − Γ p ij ∂Ap ∂xk − Γ p kj ∂Ai ∂xp +Γp ijΓ r pkAr + Γp kjΓ r piAr . Since all terms involving ˝rst and second derivatives of A cancel out, we are left with terms depending only on the Christo˙el symbols : ∇j∇kAi − ∇k∇jAi = ( ∂Γ r ki ∂xj − ∂Γ r ij ∂xk ) Ar + ( Γ p ikΓ r pj − Γ p ijΓ r pk) Ar. Here ∂Γr ki ∂xj denotes the ordinary partial derivative of the function Γr ki = Γr ki(x1, x2, x3). 23 36

# Page 28^page=28
Deriving the RiemannChristoffel tensor  Final De˝nition of curvature We therefore de˝ne the RiemannChristo˙el tensor by ∇j∇kAi − ∇k∇jAi = Rr ijkAr, where Rr ijk = ∂Γr ki ∂xj − ∂Γr ij ∂xk + Γp ikΓ r pj − Γ p ijΓ r pk. 24 36

# Page 29^page=29
The RiemannChristoffel tensor is a tensor The RiemannChristo˙el tensor is in fact a tensor Recall ∇j∇kAi − ∇k∇jAi = Rr ijkAr. (1) Let us show that Rr ijk is a tensor. Proof. Since the left-hand side of (1) is a subtraction of tensors, it is a tensor. Since the left-hand side of (1) is a tensor, so is Rr ijkAr. Because Ar is arbitrary, it follows by the quotient rule that Rr ijk is a tensor . 25 36

# Page 30^page=30
Condition for Euclidean Space Condition for Euclidean Space For Euclidean space , we need zero curvature: Ai,jk = Ai,kj. We have shown Ai,jk − Ai,kj = Rr ijkAr, so the condition for a space to be Euclidean is therefore Ai,jk = Ai,kj ⇐⇒ Ai,jk − Ai,kj = 0 ⇐⇒ Rr ijk = 0. This means that a Euclidean space must have a vanishing Riemann-Christo˙el tensor. 26 36

# Page 31^page=31
Example Example Consider the surface of the sphere of radius r = 1, which is a surface of positive curvature. The position vector is given in spherical coordinates (x1, x2) = (ϕ, θ) by r = sin ϕ cos θ i1 + sin ϕ sin θ i2 + cos ϕ i3, and thus e1 = ∂r ∂ϕ = cos ϕ cos θ i1 + cos ϕ sin θ i2 − sin ϕ i3 e2 = ∂r ∂θ = − sin ϕ sin θi1 + sin ϕ cos θ i2. We will now ˝nd the components of the Riemann-Christo˙el tensor. 27 36

# Page 32^page=32
Example - Part 2 Example Methodology: Recall Riemann-Christo˙el tensor Rr ijk = [ ∂ ∂xj Γ r ki − ∂ ∂xk Γ r ij + Γp ikΓ r pj − Γp ijΓ r pk ] . So we will need: Christo˙el symbols of second and ˝rst kind Γ i jk = 1 2 giℓ ( ∂gℓj ∂xk + ∂gℓk ∂xj − ∂gjk ∂xℓ ) , Γijk = 1 2 ( ∂gij ∂xk + ∂gik ∂xj − ∂gjk ∂xi ) . the metric tensor gij = ei · ej. 28 36

# Page 33^page=33
Example - Part 3 Example We ˝rst ˝nd the components of the metric tensor via gij = ei · ej. Using the values we found for e1 and e2 e1 = ∂r ∂ϕ = cos ϕ cos θ i1 + cos ϕ sin θ i2 − sin ϕ i3 e2 = ∂r ∂θ = − sin ϕ sin θi1 + sin ϕ cos θ i2. we get g11 = 1, g12 = 0, g22 = sin 2 ϕ. 29 36

# Page 34^page=34
Example - Part 4 Example Next we ˝nd Christo˙el symbols of the ˝rst kind using the formula Γijk = 1 2 ( ∂gij ∂xk + ∂gik ∂xj − ∂gjk ∂xi ) . Again, g11 = 1, g12 = 0, g22 = sin 2 ϕ. Thus, the only ∂gab ∂xc that is non-zero is ∂g22 ∂x1 = ∂ sin 2 ϕ ∂ϕ = 2 sin ϕ cos ϕ. We conclude that Γijk = 0, unless two indices are 2 and one index is 1. 30 36

# Page 35^page=35
Example - Part 5 Example Consequently, Γ111 = Γ112 = Γ121 = Γ112 = Γ222 = 0. Moreover, Γ122 = 1 2 ( ∂g12 ∂x2 + ∂g12 ∂x2 − ∂g22 ∂x1 ) = 1 2 (− ∂ sin 2 ϕ ∂ϕ ) = − sin ϕ cos ϕ. Using Ricci's Theorem, we obtain 0 = ∂g12 ∂x2 = Γ122 + Γ212. We conclude Γ212 = −Γ122 = sin ϕ cos ϕ. 31 36

# Page 36^page=36
Example - Part 6 Example Also, by the symmetry of the Chrito˙el symbols Γ221 = Γ212. We conclude Γ111 = Γ112 = Γ121 = Γ211 = Γ222 = 0, Γ122 = − sin ϕ cos ϕ, Γ221 = Γ212 = sin ϕ cos ϕ. Next, we ˝nd Christo˙el symbols of the second kind using Γ i jk = giℓΓℓjk. 32 36

# Page 37^page=37
Example - Part 7 Example First, we ˝nd the components of the metric tensor g11 = 1 g11 = 1, g22 = 1 g22 = 1 sin 2 ϕ , g12 = 0. Recall that Christo˙el symbols of the ˝rst kind are Γ111 = Γ112 = Γ121 = Γ211 = Γ222 = 0, Γ122 = − sin ϕ cos ϕ, Γ221 = sin ϕ cos ϕ. Thus, the Christo˙el symbols of the second kind are Γ 1 11 = Γ 1 12 = Γ 2 11 = Γ 2 22 = 0, Γ 1 22 = g1ℓΓℓ22 = g11Γ122 + g12Γ222 = − sin ϕ cos ϕ, Γ 2 12 = g2ℓΓℓ12 = g21Γ112 + g22Γ212 = cot ϕ. 33 36

# Page 38^page=38
Example - Part 8 Example The Christo˙el symbols of the second kind are Γ 1 11 = Γ 1 12 = Γ 1 21 = Γ 2 11 = Γ 2 22 = 0, Γ 1 22 = − sin ϕ cos ϕ, Γ 2 12 = Γ 2 21 = cot ϕ. Therefore, we can ˝nd the Riemann-Christo˙el tensor using the formula Rr ijk = [ ∂ ∂xj Γ r ki − ∂ ∂xk Γ r ij + Γp ikΓ r pj − Γp ijΓ r pk ] . Notice that R1 111 = R1 112 = R1 121 = R1 211 = R1 122 = R1 221 = R1 222 = 0, R2 111 = R2 211 = R2 221 = R2 122 = R2 222 = 0. 34 36

# Page 39^page=39
Example - Part 9 Example The Christo˙el symbols of the second kind are Γ 1 11 = Γ 1 12 = Γ 2 11 = Γ 2 22 = 0, Γ 1 22 = − sin ϕ cos ϕ, Γ 2 12 = cot ϕ. Moreover, R1 212 = [ ∂ ∂x1 Γ 1 22 − ∂ ∂x2 Γ 1 21 + Γp 22Γ 1 p1 − Γ p 21Γ1 p2 ] = ∂ ∂ϕ Γ1 22 − Γ 2 21Γ 1 22 = ∂ ∂ϕ (− sin ϕ cos ϕ) − cos ϕ sin ϕ (− sin ϕ cos ϕ) = − cos2 ϕ + sin2 ϕ + cos2 ϕ = sin 2 ϕ. 35 36
